title: Height & diameter

hook.scenario: To find the longest communication path between any two computers in a network tree, a developer calls `get_height(left) + get_height(right)` at every single node, causing their program to run in painfully slow O(n^2) time.
hook.question: How do you calculate tree height and global diameter simultaneously in a single O(n) pass?

why_it_exists.problem: Calculating tree height separately at every node to find the maximum diameter results in repetitive subtree traversals taking O(n^2) time.
why_it_exists.naive_solution: For every node in the tree, call a helper function `height(node.left)` and `height(node.right)`.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Use a bottom-up post-order traversal. Each recursive step returns the node's own height `1 + max(left_h, right_h)` while simultaneously updating a global diameter variable `max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left_h + right_h)`.

mental_model.intuition: Return more than you are asked: return subtree height upwards to your parent, while side-effecting global max diameter at your node.
mental_model.description: At each node, compute `left_height` and `right_height` from post-order child returns. The longest path passing THROUGH this node is `left_height + right_height` (edges). Update `global_diameter = max(global_diameter, left_height + right_height)`. Then return `1 + max(left_height, right_height)` to the parent so it can compute its own height.
mental_model.repeated_decision: at this node, combine left and right subtree HEIGHTS -- update the best diameter, then return the node's own height.

explanation:
Definitions:
- Height of a Node: Number of edges on the longest downward path to a leaf (null node height = 0 for node-count framing or -1 for edge-count framing; here we use height as depth level where null = 0).
- Diameter of a Tree: The length of the longest path between ANY two nodes in a tree (measured in number of edges). The path does NOT necessarily have to pass through the root.
- Height Invariant: `height(node) = 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))`
- Diameter-Through-Node Invariant: `diameter_at_node = height(node.left) + height(node.right)`

Why Naive O(n^2) is Bad:
`def diameter(root):`
  `if not root: return 0`
  `d_root = height(root.left) + height(root.right)`
  `return max(d_root, diameter(root.left), diameter(root.right))`
Because `height()` takes O(n) time and is called at every node, total time is O(n^2).

Optimal O(n) Single-Pass Pattern:
Maintain a non-local variable `max_diameter = 0`:
`def get_height(node):`
  `if not node: return 0`
  `left_h = get_height(node.left)`
  `right_h = get_height(node.right)`
  `max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left_h + right_h)`
  `return 1 + max(left_h, right_h)`

Walkthrough on a Skewed Tree where Diameter Dodges Root:
Tree:
        1
       /
      2
     / \
    3   4
   /     \
  5       6

- At node `3`: `left_h = 1` (leaf 5), `right_h = 0`. Returns `2`. Diameter at 3 = 1.
- At node `4`: `left_h = 0`, `right_h = 1` (leaf 6). Returns `2`. Diameter at 4 = 1.
- At node `2`: `left_h = 2` (sub-tree at 3), `right_h = 2` (sub-tree at 4).
  - Diameter through `2` = `left_h + right_h = 2 + 2 = 4` edges (path: 5 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 6).
  - `max_diameter` updated to 4!
  - Node `2` returns height `1 + max(2, 2) = 3` to root `1`.
- At root `1`: `left_h = 3`, `right_h = 0`. Diameter through root = 3. `max_diameter` remains 4!
Notice the longest path dodges root `1` completely!

Related Application - Height-Balanced Check:
The same bottom-up post-order return pattern determines if a tree is height-balanced (where subtrees of every node differ in height by at most 1). At each node, compute `left_h` and `right_h`. If `abs(left_h - right_h) > 1` (or if either child returned -1), return -1 to signal imbalance upwards immediately. Otherwise return `1 + max(left_h, right_h)`. This checks balance in O(n) time instead of naive O(n^2).

key_points.title: Post-Order Single Pass
key_points.detail: Bottom-up traversal processes children first, allowing height return and diameter update in O(n) time.

key_points.title: Root Independence
key_points.detail: Tree diameter does NOT necessarily pass through the root node.

key_points.title: Return Value vs Global Side-Effect
key_points.detail: Function return value feeds parent height calculations; global side-effect records maximum path across all nodes.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming the diameter always passes through the root
common_mistakes.explanation: In skewed or unbalanced trees, the longest path between two leaves often exists entirely inside a deep left or right subtree.

common_mistakes.title: Recomputing height at every node (O(n^2) naive trap)
common_mistakes.explanation: Calling a helper `height()` inside a recursive `diameter()` function re-traverses subtrees redundantly, ballooning runtime to O(n^2).

common_mistakes.title: Confusing edge count vs node count
common_mistakes.explanation: Edge count diameter = node count on path - 1. Pay close attention to whether the problem asks for number of edges or number of nodes.

when_not_to_use.scenario: Graphs with cycles or non-tree structures
when_not_to_use.reason: Graph diameter requires all-pairs shortest path algorithms (Floyd-Warshall or BFS from all vertices).

failure_signals: Problem asks for the longest path between any two nodes in a binary tree.
Problem asks to check if a binary tree is height-balanced.

engineering_examples.title: Network Latency Bound in Hierarchy
engineering_examples.problem: Calculate the worst-case message propagation delay between any two nodes in a hierarchical network.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Network latency is proportional to the tree diameter (the longest hop path between any two terminal nodes).

engineering_examples.title: UI Tree Layout Budgeting
engineering_examples.problem: Determine maximum depth rendering bounds for deeply nested UI trees.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Height calculations establish container layout budgets in single-pass tree passes.

recall_questions.q: What is the relationship between node height and the heights of its subtrees?
Does the diameter of a binary tree always pass through the root node?
recall_questions.answer: No. In unbalanced or skewed trees, the longest path between two leaves may lie entirely within a single deep subtree.

recall_questions.q: Why is computing diameter in a single post-order pass O(n) instead of O(n^2)?
recall_questions.answer: Because each node computes its height and updates the running max diameter simultaneously in one pass, without re-traversing subtrees.

oa_questions.question: Diameter of Binary Tree: Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of the diameter of the tree in edges.
oa_questions.answer: Use post-order DFS helper that returns height `1 + max(left, right)` and updates global `max_diameter = max(max_diameter, left + right)`. Return `max_diameter`.
oa_questions.approach: Single-pass bottom-up post-order DFS with global max tracker.

oa_questions.question: Balanced Binary Tree: Determine if a binary tree is height-balanced (subtrees of every node differ in height by at most 1).
oa_questions.answer: Use post-order DFS helper returning height. If `abs(left_h - right_h) > 1`, return -1 to signal imbalance upwards early.
oa_questions.approach: Post-order bottom-up DFS returning -1 on imbalance.

interesting_facts: The exact same single-pass pattern (returning max branch path while updating global path sum) is used to solve LeetCode Hard 'Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum'.
